docs.title: AWS Small MLOps Platform
docs.text: An open-source AWS MLOps platform built with Terraform, Python, and automated testing. It provides a modular foundation for secure, scalable, and reproducible cloud infrastructure, with CI/CD workflows, infrastructure validation, documentation, and release automation.

docs.title: Project Goals
docs.text:
• Build reusable AWS infrastructure using Terraform.
  • Establish secure and reproducible infrastructure provisioning.
  • Validate infrastructure code through automated testing.
  • Automate code quality checks and CI/CD workflows.
  • Maintain versioned documentation and releases.

docs.title: Development
docs.text: Start with the Getting Started guide to configure the local development environment and run the initial checks.

docs.title: Project Status
docs.text: The project is currently establishing its development environment, testing conventions, and automation foundations. Infrastructure modules and deployment workflows will be introduced incrementally.

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text: This guide explains how to configure the local development environment for the AWS Small MLOps Platform.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Install the following tools:

  • Git
  • Python version supported by pyproject.toml
  • uv
  • OpenTofu CLI
  • pre-commit — installed through the project environment

Verify the installations:

python --version
uv --version
tofu version
git --version

docs.title: Clone the Repository
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/Rahul-Shelke-1/aws-mlops-small-iac01-tf.git
cd aws-mlops-small-iac01-tf

docs.title: Set Up the Python Environment
docs.text:
Install the project dependencies and create the virtual environment:

uv sync

This installs dependencies declared in pyproject.toml and uses uv.lock to reproduce the resolved environment.

If development dependencies are configured in a separate dependency group, install them using the appropriate command, such as:

uv sync --group dev

Activate the environment if you prefer working inside it interactively:

source .venv/bin/activate

Alternatively, execute project commands using uv run without activating the environment.

Verify the development tools:

uv run pre-commit --version
uv run pytest --version

docs.title: Configure Pre-commit
docs.text:
Install the repository's Git hooks:

uv run pre-commit install

Run all configured hooks against the repository:

uv run pre-commit run --all-files

Resolve any reported issues before committing changes.

If secret detection is configured to use .secrets.baseline, initialize the baseline when it does not already exist:

uv run detect-secrets scan > .secrets.baseline

Review the baseline carefully before committing it. Never treat actual credentials as acceptable findings.

docs.title: OpenTofu Development
docs.text:
OpenTofu is used to manage the platform's infrastructure as code.

Verify the installation:

tofu version

Format OpenTofu configuration files:

tofu fmt -recursive

Check formatting without modifying files:

tofu fmt -check -recursive

Before validating a particular infrastructure root module, change into its directory and initialize it:

cd path/to/infrastructure/root
tofu init
tofu validate

Replace the example directory with the actual infrastructure root module.

Run tofu plan only when you are ready to evaluate the proposed infrastructure changes. AWS credentials and appropriate permissions may be required, depending on the providers and data sources configured.

Do not run tofu apply against a shared or production environment without following the project's deployment and approval procedures.

docs.title: Run Tests
docs.text: The project uses pytest for Python tests and OpenTofu for infrastructure management.

docs.title: Run the Complete Test Suite
docs.text: uv run pytest

docs.title: Run Unit Tests
docs.text:
uv run pytest tests/unit/

Unit tests should validate Python logic and project configuration without provisioning infrastructure.

docs.title: Run Integration Tests
docs.text:
uv run pytest tests/integration/

The initial integration test verifies that the OpenTofu CLI is installed and executable.

Future integration tests may validate Terraform-compatible infrastructure configurations using tftest or OpenTofu's native testing capabilities.

docs.title: Run OpenTofu Formatting Checks
docs.text: tofu fmt -check -recursive

docs.title: Run Pre-commit Checks
docs.text:
uv run pre-commit run --all-files

Integration tests that interact with AWS or provision infrastructure may require credentials, permissions, initialized modules, and isolated test resources. Do not run infrastructure tests against production environments without explicit safeguards.

docs.title: Development Workflow
docs.text:
1. Create a focused feature or chore branch.
  2. Implement the change and add relevant tests.
  3. Run pre-commit hooks and the applicable test suite locally.
  4. Commit changes using Conventional Commits.
  5. Open a pull request and ensure the required checks pass.
  6. Merge the pull request after review and required checks succeed.

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text: Future development will introduce OpenTofu CI, Python-based infrastructure testing, documentation preview and deployment, and automated releases.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The Small MLOps Platform uses GitHub Actions to automate code quality checks, Python testing, infrastructure validation, documentation publishing, and release management.

The CI/CD strategy is designed to establish reliable validation and delivery practices before implementing the AWS infrastructure layers. Each workflow has a clearly defined responsibility, allowing changes to be validated independently and integrated through pull requests.

docs.title: Objectives
docs.text:
The CI/CD foundation aims to:

  • Automate code quality and security checks.
  • Validate Python code and tests across supported Python versions.
  • Validate OpenTofu configurations before infrastructure deployment.
  • Build and publish project documentation.
  • Standardize release versioning and changelog generation.
  • Establish a foundation for secure, controlled infrastructure delivery.

docs.title: Workflow Architecture
docs.text:
The CI/CD system is organized into four initial workflows.

Workflow Responsibility Status Python CI Code quality, security checks, and automated tests Implemented OpenTofu CI Infrastructure formatting, validation, linting, and security checks Planned Documentation Deployment Documentation build validation and GitHub Pages publishing Planned Release Workflow Automated release PRs, changelogs, and version management Planned Infrastructure CD Controlled infrastructure planning, approval, and deployment Future

Workflow status should be updated as each implementation is completed and merged.

docs.title: Development and Integration Workflow
docs.text:
The repository follows a feature-branch workflow.

  1. Create a feature branch from the latest main.
  2. Implement a focused change.
  3. Run relevant checks locally.
  4. Open a pull request targeting main.
  5. Review the changes and verify the required CI checks.
  6. Merge the pull request after successful validation.

This approach keeps changes isolated, makes failures easier to diagnose, and provides a consistent review process.

docs.title: Continuous Integration
docs.text:
Continuous Integration (CI) validates changes before they are merged.

The initial CI capabilities include:

  • Python formatting and linting.
  • Static type checking.
  • Python security scanning.
  • Unit and integration testing.
  • OpenTofu configuration validation.

Workflows are triggered by relevant repository changes and pull requests according to their configured branch and path filters.

docs.title: Continuous Delivery and Deployment
docs.text:
Documentation publishing and release automation are planned as separate workflows.

Infrastructure deployment will be implemented later, when the bootstrap layer and its validation strategy are ready.

The intended infrastructure delivery process will include:

  • OpenTofu plan generation and review.
  • Environment-specific configuration.
  • Secure AWS authentication using GitHub Actions OIDC.
  • Approval and protection rules for sensitive environments.
  • Controlled application of infrastructure changes.

Infrastructure CD will not be enabled until the required infrastructure configuration, state management, permissions, and deployment safeguards are in place.

docs.title: Security Principles
docs.text:
The CI/CD implementation follows these principles:

  • Use least-privilege GitHub Actions permissions.
  • Avoid storing long-lived AWS credentials in repository secrets when OIDC federation is suitable.
  • Keep secrets out of source code and workflow logs.
  • Validate infrastructure changes before applying them.
  • Require review and appropriate approvals for sensitive changes.
  • Separate validation from deployment responsibilities.

docs.title: Related Documentation
docs.text:
• Python CI
  • OpenTofu CI — planned
  • Documentation Deployment — planned
  • Release Workflow — planned
  • Infrastructure CD — documentation to be added as the deployment design matures.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The project uses GitHub Actions to automate documentation validation, preview deployment, and versioned documentation publishing.

Two independent workflows handle the documentation lifecycle:

  • Documentation Preview — builds and deploys documentation previews for pull requests using Cloudflare Pages.
  • Documentation Release — publishes versioned documentation using MkDocs and Mike, with the generated site hosted through GitHub Pages.

This separation allows documentation changes to be reviewed before merging while preserving versioned documentation for published releases.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    A[Documentation Changes] --> B{Pull Request or Main?}

    B -->|Pull Request to main| C[docs-preview.yml]
    C --> D[Install Python and uv]
    D --> E[Strict MkDocs Build]
    E --> F{Build Successful?}
    F -->|No| G[Fail CI]
    F -->|Yes| H[Upload HTML Artifact]
    H --> I[Deploy Preview to Cloudflare Pages]
    I --> J[Comment Preview URL on PR]

    B -->|Push to main| K[docs-release.yml]
    B -->|Published GitHub Release| K

    K --> L[Install Dependencies]
    L --> M{Trigger Type}
    M -->|Push to main| N[Update latest]
    M -->|Published Release| O[Deploy Release Version]
    O --> P[Update latest Alias]
    N --> Q[Publish to gh-pages]
    P --> Q
    Q --> R[GitHub Pages]

docs.title: 1. Documentation Preview Workflow
docs.text: Workflow: .github/workflows/docs-preview.yml

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: The preview workflow validates documentation changes and creates a temporary preview before the pull request is merged into main.

docs.title: Trigger Conditions
docs.text:
The workflow runs when a pull request targets main and changes relevant files, including:

  • docs/**
  • mkdocs.yml
  • pyproject.toml
  • uv.lock
  • .github/workflows/**

The path filters should include the preview workflow itself so changes to its configuration can be tested.

docs.title: Execution Steps
docs.text:
1. Check out the pull request source code.
  2. Install uv and configure dependency caching.
  3. Set up Python 3.11.
  4. Build the documentation using strict validation.
  5. Upload the generated HTML as a workflow artifact.
  6. Deploy the preview to Cloudflare Pages.
  7. Comment on the pull request with the preview URL and source commit SHA.

docs.title: Strict Documentation Build
docs.text:
uv run mkdocs build --strict

Strict mode treats MkDocs warnings as build failures. This helps detect issues such as broken internal links and invalid documentation configuration before deployment.

The generated website is written to the site/ directory.

docs.title: Preview Hosting
docs.text:
The workflow deploys the generated site to the Cloudflare Pages project:

github-docs-preview

The preview URL is returned by the deployment action and included in a pull request comment.

docs.title: Required GitHub Secrets
docs.text:
Configure the following repository secrets:

Secret Purpose CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN Authenticates Cloudflare deployment requests CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID Identifies the Cloudflare account

The Cloudflare API token should have only the permissions required to deploy to the intended Pages project.

docs.title: Note:
docs.text:
In the Cloudflare token creation screen, select:

Field Recommended value Permission category Account Permission Cloudflare Pages — Edit Account resources Include → your specific Cloudflare account

If the permission dropdown displays Cloudflare Pages, select Edit rather than Read.

docs.title: Expected Outcome
docs.text: A pull request receives a preview link that reviewers can use to verify navigation, page rendering, formatting, and content before approving the changes.

docs.title: 2. Documentation Release Workflow
docs.text: Workflow: .github/workflows/docs-release.yml

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
The release workflow publishes documentation to GitHub Pages and maintains multiple documentation versions using Mike.

It supports two deployment paths.

docs.title: Deployment Strategies
docs.text: Trigger Action Version behavior Push to main Update documentation Refresh the latest alias Published GitHub release Publish release documentation Deploy the release version and point latest to it

docs.title: Push to Main
docs.text:
Documentation changes merged into main can update the existing latest documentation without creating a new version.

uv run mike deploy --push latest
uv run mike set-default --push latest

This is intended for documentation-only corrections, such as typo fixes and minor clarifications.

docs.title: Published Release
docs.text:
When a GitHub release is published, the workflow should use the release tag to build and publish the corresponding documentation version.

For example, publishing release v1.2.0 should produce a versioned documentation entry for v1.2.0 and update the latest alias.

uv run mike deploy --push --update-aliases 1.2.0 latest
uv run mike set-default --push latest

The version supplied to Mike should follow the project's chosen version naming convention. If Git tags include the v prefix, ensure the workflow consistently handles it.

Important: The workflow must check out the release tag when processing a published release. Otherwise, it may accidentally build documentation from the current branch rather than the released source code.

docs.title: GitHub Pages Publishing
docs.text:
Mike maintains versioned documentation in the gh-pages branch. The workflow requires Git write permissions to push these updates.

The generated site should expose:

  • A version-specific documentation URL.
  • A latest alias for the most recently published release.
  • A default landing page that redirects to or selects latest.

The gh-pages branch is a deployment artifact branch; it should not be used for application source development.

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text:
Ensure the project includes the required MkDocs and Mike dependencies in pyproject.toml.

For example:

[project]
dependencies = [
    "mkdocs",
    "mike",
]

This is illustrative only. Preserve the project's existing dependencies and dependency groups, and configure the actual versions and MkDocs theme/plugins required by the repository.

After changing dependencies, update the lockfile:

uv lock

docs.title: MkDocs Configuration
docs.text:
Review mkdocs.yml to ensure the site configuration supports the selected theme, plugins, navigation, and version selector.

For versioned documentation, verify that the theme integrates with Mike's version metadata and that the default version behavior is appropriate.

docs.title: GitHub Actions Permissions
docs.text:
Use the minimum permissions necessary for each workflow.

For the preview workflow, permissions may include:

  • contents: read
  • pull-requests: write for posting preview comments.
  • deployments: write only if required by the deployment action and integration.

For the release workflow, contents: write is required to publish changes to gh-pages.

Do not grant broad repository permissions when narrower permissions are sufficient.

docs.title: 4. Deployment Lifecycle
docs.text:
The expected documentation lifecycle is:

  1. Create a feature branch for documentation changes.
  2. Update the Markdown files, navigation, or MkDocs configuration.
  3. Open a pull request against main.
  4. Allow the preview workflow to build, validate, and deploy the documentation.
  5. Review the preview and resolve any build warnings or content issues.
  6. Merge the approved pull request.
  7. Allow the release workflow to update latest.
  8. When a software release is published, deploy the corresponding versioned documentation and update the latest alias.

This process makes documentation validation part of the standard development workflow.

docs.title: 5. Local Validation
docs.text: Before opening a pull request, validate the documentation locally.

docs.title: Install Dependencies
docs.text: uv sync --locked

docs.title: Run the Local Documentation Server
docs.text: uv run mkdocs serve

docs.title: Build Documentation Strictly
docs.text: uv run mkdocs build --strict

docs.title: Inspect the Generated Site
docs.text:
ls site/

Resolve build warnings and verify the site before submitting changes.

docs.title: 6. Troubleshooting
docs.text: Problem Possible cause Recommended action Strict build fails Broken links, invalid configuration, or warnings Review the build output and correct the underlying issues Cloudflare deployment fails Invalid token, missing secret, or insufficient permissions Verify repository secrets and Cloudflare token permissions Pull request comment is missing Comment action failed or permissions are insufficient Inspect workflow logs and verify pull-requests: write Versioned deployment fails Missing gh-pages history or Git write access Check checkout depth, branch access, and workflow permissions Release publishes the wrong documentation Workflow builds the wrong Git ref Explicitly check out the release tag latest points to the wrong version Incorrect Mike alias or default-version configuration Verify the deployment command and default-version update Preview deployment overwrites production Preview and production share an unintended deployment target Verify the Cloudflare Pages project and GitHub Pages configuration

docs.title: 7. Security and Operational Considerations
docs.text:
• Store deployment credentials in GitHub repository or environment secrets.
  • Never commit Cloudflare API tokens or other credentials.
  • Use least-privilege permissions for GitHub Actions.
  • Pin third-party actions to reviewed versions or immutable commit SHAs according to the repository's security policy.
  • Validate documentation before deploying it.
  • Test release and patch deployment paths independently.
  • Avoid exposing sensitive information in documentation previews.
  • Review deployment logs when a workflow fails.

docs.title: 8. Definition of Done
docs.text:
Documentation deployment is operational when:

  • Pull requests trigger strict documentation validation.
  • Successful builds generate and upload the HTML artifact.
  • Cloudflare Pages previews are accessible from pull request comments.
  • Pushes to main update the intended latest documentation.
  • Published releases create the corresponding versioned documentation.
  • The default documentation entry points to latest.
  • Deployment credentials and permissions follow least-privilege principles.
  • Both workflows have been tested independently.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• MkDocs Documentation
  • Mike — Manage multiple versions of documentation
  • GitHub Actions Documentation
  • Cloudflare Pages Documentation
  • GitHub Pages Documentation

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Python CI automates code quality checks, security scanning, and automated testing for the Small MLOps Platform.

The workflow is implemented using GitHub Actions and uses uv for Python installation and dependency management.

Workflow file: .github/workflows/python-ci.yml

docs.title: Objectives
docs.text:
• Enforce consistent Python code formatting.
  • Detect common code-quality issues.
  • Perform static type checking.
  • Scan Python code for common security issues.
  • Execute unit and integration tests.
  • Validate compatibility across supported Python versions.

docs.title: Workflow Triggers
docs.text:
The workflow supports the following triggers:

Trigger Behavior Push to main Runs when configured path filters match Push to feat/** Runs when configured path filters match Push to fix/** Runs when configured path filters match Pull request targeting main Runs when configured path filters match Manual dispatch Allows manual execution

The workflow uses path filters to avoid running for changes unrelated to Python CI.

The configured paths are:

  • tests/**
  • pyproject.toml
  • uv.lock
  • .pre-commit-config.yaml
  • .github/workflows/python-ci.yml

These paths must remain synchronized with the actual workflow configuration.

docs.title: Code Quality and Security
docs.text: The quality job runs on Ubuntu using Python 3.11.

docs.title: Formatting
docs.text:
Ruff checks whether Python files follow the configured formatting rules.

uv run ruff format --check .

The check reports formatting differences without modifying files.

docs.title: Linting
docs.text:
Ruff detects common programming errors and code-quality issues.

uv run ruff check .

docs.title: Static Type Checking
docs.text:
mypy checks type annotations and reports potential type inconsistencies.

uv run mypy tests/

docs.title: Security Scanning
docs.text:
Bandit scans Python code for common security issues.

uv run bandit -r tests/

These commands target the test directory. Tool rules and exclusions can be managed through the project's configuration where applicable.

docs.title: Automated Testing
docs.text: The test job runs after the quality job succeeds.

docs.title: Python Version Matrix
docs.text:
Tests execute against the supported Python versions:

  • Python 3.11
  • Python 3.12
  • Python 3.13

The matrix helps identify compatibility issues across supported interpreter versions.

docs.title: Unit Tests
docs.text:
Unit tests validate individual functions, classes, and components.

Test directory: tests/unit/

uv run pytest tests/unit

docs.title: Integration Tests
docs.text:
Integration tests validate interactions between components and their dependencies.

Test directory: tests/integration/

uv run pytest tests/integration

Integration tests that require external services or cloud resources must use explicitly configured test fixtures, local services, or dedicated test environments.

docs.title: Dependency Management
docs.text:
The workflow uses uv to install Python and synchronize project dependencies.

The following files define the project's dependency configuration:

  • pyproject.toml
  • uv.lock

Development dependencies must include the tools required by the workflow, including Ruff, mypy, Bandit, and pytest.

The lockfile should be committed and kept synchronized with dependency changes.

docs.title: Local Validation
docs.text:
Before opening a pull request, run the relevant checks locally.

uv run ruff format --check tests/
uv run ruff check tests/
uv run mypy tests/
uv run bandit -r tests/
uv run pytest tests/unit
uv run pytest tests/integration

To correct formatting issues locally, run:

uv run ruff format tests/

Resolve reported issues before pushing changes.

docs.title: Failure Handling
docs.text:
If a workflow fails:

  1. Open the failed GitHub Actions run.
  2. Identify the failed job and step.
  3. Reproduce the failure locally when possible.
  4. Correct the underlying issue.
  5. Run the relevant checks again.
  6. Push the fix and verify the updated workflow run.

Pull requests should be merged only after the required checks pass and the changes have been reviewed.

docs.title: Future Improvements
docs.text:
Potential extensions to Python CI include:

  • Uploading test results and coverage reports.
  • Enforcing a minimum test coverage threshold.
  • Publishing machine-readable test reports.
  • Adding dependency vulnerability scanning.
  • Integrating CI checks with branch protection rules.

These improvements should be introduced when they provide clear value to the project.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The release workflow automates version management, changelog generation, and GitHub Releases using Release Please.

It runs through GitHub Actions whenever changes are pushed to the main branch. Release Please analyzes Conventional Commit messages and creates or updates a release pull request containing the proposed version and changelog updates.

When the release pull request is merged, Release Please publishes the corresponding GitHub Release and creates a Git tag.

docs.title: Objectives
docs.text:
• Automate semantic versioning and release management.
  • Generate changelog entries from Conventional Commits.
  • Maintain a traceable history of platform changes.
  • Publish versioned GitHub Releases.
  • Keep release management consistent across infrastructure and testing code.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
The repository uses a single release stream for the platform. Infrastructure code under /infra and Python testing code under /test contribute to the same release history.

flowchart TD
    A[Changes to infra or test] --> B[Conventional Commits]
    B --> C[Merge changes into main]
    C --> D[Release Please GitHub Action]
    D --> E[Create or update release PR]
    E --> F{Release PR merged?}
    F -- No --> E
    F -- Yes --> G[Update version and changelog]
    G --> H[Create Git tag]
    H --> I[Publish GitHub Release]

docs.title: Workflow Configuration
docs.text:
The workflow is defined in .github/workflows/release-please.yml.

name: release-please

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main
  workflow_dispatch:

permissions:
  contents: write
  pull-requests: write
  issues: write

jobs:
  release-please:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: release-please-oss/release-please-action@v5
        id: release
        with:
          token: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
          release-type: simple

docs.title: Triggers
docs.text: Trigger Behavior Push to main Evaluates commits and creates or updates a release pull request when appropriate. Manual dispatch Allows the workflow to be run manually from GitHub Actions.

docs.title: Permissions
docs.text:
Permission Purpose contents: write Allows repository content, Git tags, and releases to be managed. pull-requests: write Allows Release Please to create and update release pull requests. issues: write Allows issue-related operations required by the configured action.

The workflow uses the repository-provided GITHUB_TOKEN. Grant only the permissions required by the release process.

docs.title: Versioning Strategy
docs.text:
The platform follows Semantic Versioning:

MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH

Version component Meaning Example MAJOR Incompatible or breaking changes 1.0.0 → 2.0.0 MINOR Backward-compatible functionality 1.0.0 → 1.1.0 PATCH Backward-compatible bug fixes 1.0.0 → 1.0.1

Release Please uses Conventional Commit messages to determine the proposed version increment.

The simple release strategy is intended for a repository-level release, rather than independent releases for individual folders. The infrastructure and testing code therefore share a release version and changelog.

docs.title: Conventional Commits
docs.text:
Use Conventional Commits for changes merged into main.

The general format is:

<type>(<scope>): <description>

docs.title: Supported examples
docs.text:
Commit message Expected effect feat(infra): add VPC module Feature; normally a minor version increment. fix(infra): correct S3 bucket policy Bug fix; normally a patch increment. feat(test): add infrastructure integration tests Feature; normally a minor version increment. feat(ci): add release automation Feature; normally a minor version increment. feat(infra)!: change module interface Breaking change; normally a major version increment. docs(cicd): document release workflow Documentation change; normally no version increment. chore(ci): update action versions Maintenance change; normally no version increment.

A commit marked with ! indicates a breaking change. A BREAKING CHANGE: footer can also communicate breaking changes.

Actual version increments depend on the configured release strategy, commit parsing, and release history. Verify the generated release pull request before merging it.

docs.title: 1. Develop and merge changes
docs.text:
Create a feature or fix branch, implement the change, and open a pull request targeting main.

Use meaningful Conventional Commit messages. Ensure the relevant CI checks pass before merging.

docs.title: 2. Evaluate commits
docs.text:
After changes reach main, the Release Please workflow evaluates the commit history since the previous release.

If a release is warranted, it creates or updates a release pull request containing the proposed version and changelog changes.

docs.title: 3. Review the release pull request
docs.text:
Review the generated pull request before merging it.

Check that:

  • The proposed version increment is appropriate.
  • The changelog accurately describes the changes.
  • Breaking changes are clearly documented.
  • Infrastructure and testing changes are represented correctly.

Do not merge a release pull request until its generated changes have been reviewed.

docs.title: 4. Publish the release
docs.text:
When the release pull request is merged, Release Please creates the Git tag and publishes the corresponding GitHub Release.

The release provides a versioned reference to the platform's source code and a record of the changes included in that version.

docs.title: Changelog Management
docs.text:
The CHANGELOG.md file records changes associated with published releases.

Release Please generates release notes primarily from Conventional Commit messages. Commits such as feat: and fix: generally appear as user-facing changes, while maintenance and documentation commits may be omitted from release notes.

The changelog is updated through the generated release pull request rather than by manually editing it for every commit.

For the simple release strategy, configure the initial version file and changelog according to the Release Please setup. Keep these files at the repository root unless the release configuration specifies otherwise.

docs.title: Repository Structure
docs.text:
Relevant files for release management:

.
├── .github/
│   └── workflows/
│       └── release-please.yml
├── infra/
├── test/
├── CHANGELOG.md
├── version.txt
└── docs/
    └── cicd/
        └── release-workflow.md

version.txt and CHANGELOG.md are the expected root-level files for the recommended simple release strategy. Ensure the initial version file is initialized before relying on automated releases.

docs.title: Security and Operational Considerations
docs.text:
• Use the minimum permissions required by Release Please.
  • Protect main with branch protection rules and required CI checks.
  • Review generated release pull requests before merging.
  • Do not store personal access tokens or other credentials directly in workflow files.
  • Be aware that workflows triggered by GITHUB_TOKEN generally do not trigger other workflows. If downstream release automation is needed, evaluate a GitHub App token or appropriately scoped personal access token.
  • Test release behavior in a controlled manner before relying on it for production infrastructure changes.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Problem What to check No release pull request appears Confirm that commits follow Conventional Commits and contain release-triggering changes. Version increment is unexpected Review commit types, breaking-change markers, and the release strategy. Changelog is incomplete Check the commit messages and Release Please configuration. GitHub Release is not published Verify that the release pull request was merged and the workflow has the required permissions. A downstream workflow does not run Check whether it depends on an event generated using GITHUB_TOKEN.

docs.text:

  • Release Please GitHub Action
  • Conventional Commits
  • Semantic Versioning
